report:
### Conclusion
Contrary to your expectation, high-quality clinical evidence shows that the answer is **yes**: heavy current and former smokers who regularly participate in low-dose computed tomography (LDCT) screening are **significantly less likely to die of lung cancer**.

### Evidence
1. **National Lung Screening Trial (NLST):** This landmark trial enrolled over 53,000 high-risk current and former heavy smokers. It demonstrated a **20% reduction** in lung cancer mortality among participants who received annual low-dose CT screening compared to those screened with standard chest radiography.
2. **NELSON Trial:** A major European randomized trial published in *The New England Journal of Medicine* confirmed these benefits. It showed that volume CT screening reduced lung cancer mortality by **24% in high-risk men** and **33% in women** compared to an unscreened control group.
3. **Medical Guidelines:** Because LDCT detects lung malignancies at earlier, more treatable stages before symptoms appear, major health authorities—including the United States Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF)—recommend annual LDCT screening for high-risk adults (ages 50–80 with a 20 pack-year smoking history).

### Sources
- **NLST Trial Results:** https://msrads.web.unc.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/15695/2018/08/Lung-Cancer-Screening-NEJM.pdf
- **NELSON Trial Results:** https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1911793
- **USPSTF Screening Recommendations:** https://www.uspreventiveservicestaskforce.org/uspstf/recommendation/lung-cancer-screening
